svg.title: Topology spread constraints — anti-affinity could only say "none here"; this says "how many"

g.text: Topology spread constraints — anti-affinity could only say "none here"; this says "how many"
WHY ANTI-AFFINITY WAS NOT ENOUGH
THE FIELD — spec.topologySpreadConstraints
SKEW — the whole idea in one subtraction
whenUnsatisfiable — the required/preferred distinction, renamed
WHAT YOU GET FOR FREE, AND WHAT BITES
podAntiAffinity is a yes/no rule, and neither answer is what you usually want.
required → only ONE Pod per topology domain, ever. Replica four on a three-node
cluster is Pending forever, even though a second Pod per node is fine.
preferred → you lose the ability to ENFORCE anything at all. Five replicas may
still end up 4 + 1 if the scores happen to fall that way.
There is no way to say 'spread them, but up to two per node is acceptable'.
That number is exactly what topology spread constraints add.
topologySpreadConstraints:
- maxSkew: 1 ← REQUIRED, must be > 0. The allowed imbalance.
topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname ← the same idea as pod affinity's topologyKey
whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule ← DoNotSchedule (the DEFAULT) or ScheduleAnyway
labelSelector: ← which Pods are COUNTED
matchLabels: {app: web}
minDomains: 3 ← optional; DoNotSchedule only
nodeAffinityPolicy: Honor ← optional; Honor (default) or Ignore
nodeTaintsPolicy: Ignore ← optional; Ignore is the default
Only ONE constraint per (topologyKey, whenUnsatisfiable) pair. Same key twice is legal
only if the two entries differ in whenUnsatisfiable.
skew = matching Pods in THIS domain − the GLOBAL MINIMUM across all domains
Three zones holding 2, 2 and 1 matching Pods. The global minimum is 1.
zoneA skew = 2 − 1 = 1 zoneB skew = 2 − 1 = 1 zoneC skew = 1 − 1 = 0
With maxSkew: 1 a new Pod may go to any of the three — none would exceed 1.
Put two more into zoneA and it becomes 4, 2, 1: skew 3, which maxSkew: 1 forbids.
maxSkew: 1 is 'as even as arithmetic allows'. Larger values buy slack: with 5 Pods
over 2 nodes, maxSkew: 1 permits 3+2 and forbids 4+1.
DoNotSchedule
(the default) a FILTER. The Pod stays Pending rather than break the skew.
ScheduleAnyway
a SCORE. The Pod is placed, preferring domains that reduce skew.
Same hard/soft split as requiredDuringScheduling vs preferredDuringScheduling —
filtering versus scoring, one more time (chapter 05-05). Only the spelling changed.
Cluster-level defaults apply even if you write nothing
(stable since v1.24):
maxSkew 3 over kubernetes.io/hostname, ScheduleAnyway
maxSkew 5 over topology.kubernetes.io/zone, ScheduleAnyway
So the scheduler already nudges Pods apart. Spelling a constraint out is how you tighten it.
Known limitations worth remembering:
· Constraints are checked at SCHEDULING TIME ONLY. Scaling a Deployment DOWN can
leave the distribution imbalanced, and nothing fixes it (the Descheduler is the tool).
· The scheduler only knows domains that CURRENTLY HAVE NODES — a node pool scaled
to zero is not a domain it will try to fill.
· A Pod whose own labels do not match its labelSelector becomes a 'ghost pod': it does
not count itself, and such Pods silently pile up. Make the Pod match its own selector.
podAffinity packs, podAntiAffinity repels, topologySpreadConstraints BALANCE. The first two answer "may this Pod go here"; the third answers "how far out of balance is the cluster allowed to get".
All three use a topologyKey, and all three are evaluated only when a Pod is scheduled — none of them ever moves a Pod that is already running.
